newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire/Congo asks Zambia to end railway blockade.
newsitem.headline: Zaire/Congo asks Zambia to end railway blockade.

text.p: The new authorities in Zaire have sent a delegation to Zambia to try to persuade the Zambians to let trains cross the border, the Zairean official in charge of transport and communications said on Monday.

It has also sent a delegation to sort out a highly politicised dispute with the South African state railway company Spoornet, a partner in the company which managed the railways in southern and eastern Zaire until early this month.

Zambia stopped cross-border railway traffic this month because of a dispute over debts, freezing exports of Zairean copper and cobalt and seriously disrupting commercial life in the southern province of Katanga.

Aubert-Kizito Ntite-Mukendi, commissioner for transport and communications in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi, told Reuters in an interview, "Zambia...has blocked all the wagons and goods of Congolese clients. We've asked them to lift this embargo."

The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), the rebel movement which now runs Zaire, has stripped Sizarail, an affiliate of South African company Spoornet of its mandate to run the railways because it did not like its management style.
Management has reverted to the state-owned Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer Congolais (SNCC), the renamed version of the old Zairean state railway company SNCZ.
Mukendi, an AFDL member said "(Zambia) sent us a fax to say that Sizarail owes them about $600,000 and that if it is not paid, they'll block the goods.
"But Zambia Railways owed SNCZ $755,000. What we'll do is simply to say you take the $600,000 and give me $155,000. That's why I say the problem will be solved," he said.
SNCC officials said that delegation, led by the SNCC deputy director-general, started talks with Zambia Railways in the central town of Kabwe on Monday. They could return on Tuesday.

The decision to end the agreement with Sizarail has been widely interpreted as a unilateral and hasty nationalisation of the railways by AFDL leader Laurent Kabila, who has proclaimed himself head of state of the country.
Western commentators have said the move could augur ill for the economic policy of Kabila, who began his political life in the 1960s as a leftist and was once a Marxist.
But Mukendi and SNCC officials disputed this, saying the Zairean state company had never sold its assets to Sizarail, which had only a management contract to run the railway.

Asked to explain the decision, Mukendi said: "We found that we were the owners of the house but the tenants were doing everything possible to become the owners, so that the railways could be privatised. We said no, impossible.
"One practice we saw was that SNCC no longer had any revenue. It was Sizarail which had the revenue.

"It should have paid (to SNCC) $1 million a month and 30 percent of its profits at the end of the year. Sizarail was taking from the millions a part to pay the debts of SNCZ and was giving SNCZ $100,000, $200,000 or $300,000 -- and with that SNCZ could no longer pay salaries and current costs."

He said the new authorities also objected to the high tariffs Sizarail was charging for carrying types of goods which once had preferential treatment for social reasons, such as maize produced by small farmers.
Zaire will ask the South Africans how much Zaire owes them and how they can repay the money, he added.
